The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). A **finite-mode regulator** in this item is a fixed
finite nonempty label set $J$ with $N:=|J|\ge1$, a fixed enumeration of $J$ by
$\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and the real coordinate vector
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may name sites of a finite
lattice or finitely many modes; their geometry enters only through the chosen
polynomial below. No limit in $N$ is part of this definition.

Choose real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$, constants $c>0$ and $C_0\ge0$,
and a real polynomial $V\in\mathbb R[q_1,\ldots,q_N]$ such that
$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$
Let $H_N:=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with vectors identified up to almost
everywhere equality and inner product
$$\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}u(q)\overline{v(q)}\,dq,$$
linear in the first variable. Under Countable Choice this is a complex Hilbert
space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let
$D_0:=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, the smooth compactly supported
complex-valued functions. The associated **polynomial differential expression**
is the map
$$h_0:D_0\to H_N,\qquad h_0u:=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Vu.$$
It is well defined because each derivative of $u$ and the product $Vu$ are
smooth and compactly supported. Set $W:=V+C_0+1$, so
$W(q)\ge1+c|q|^2$. This definition specifies finite mathematical data and a
differential expression; it does not choose a self-adjoint operator domain or
assert a continuum or infinite-volume limit.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. Then $C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is dense in
$L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

derivations.claim: Since $W+1\ge2$ and every $a_j>0$, $a$ is a Hermitian positive-definite sesquilinear form on $D_0$: in particular $a(u,u)=\sum_j a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2\ge2\|u\|_2^2$, and $a(u,u)=0$ forces $u=0$ in $H_N$. Thus its Cauchy-sequence completion with the stated equivalence relation is a well-defined inner-product space.

To see that the completion is complete, let $(X_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence of its classes. By [A1], choose $u_n\in D_0$ with $\|[u_n]-X_n\|_Q<2^{-n}$ for each $n$. The triangle inequality makes $(u_n)$ $Q$-Cauchy; its class $X$ is defined by the Cauchy-sequence construction, and $\|X_n-X\|_Q\le2^{-n}+\|[u_n]-X\|_Q\to0$. Hence $Q$ is complete and therefore Hilbert.

For a $Q$-Cauchy representative sequence $(u_n)$, the inequalities $\|u_n-u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, $\sqrt{a_j}\|\partial_j u_n-\partial_j u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, and $\|\sqrt{W+1}(u_n-u_m)\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$ show that $u_n$, each $\partial_j u_n$, and $\sqrt{W+1}u_n$ converge in $L^2$ by [F2]; write their limits as $u$, $g_j$, and $h$. The first limit defines a continuous map $Q\to H_N$, since $\|u\|_2\le\|[u_n]\|_Q$, and equivalent Cauchy sequences have the same $L^2$ limit.

For every $\varphi\in D_0$, integration by parts gives $\int u_n\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int (\partial_j u_n)\overline\varphi$. Passing to the limit in both integrals by $L^2$ convergence and Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\int u\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$, so $g_j$ is the stated weak derivative.

On each compact ball $B_R$, the continuous polynomial $W+1$ is bounded. Therefore $\sqrt{W+1}u_n\to\sqrt{W+1}u$ in $L^2(B_R)$, while the same sequence converges there to $h$; uniqueness of limits gives $h=\sqrt{W+1}u$ almost everywhere on every integer-radius ball and hence almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^N$. Taking limits of the component norms in $a(u_n,u_n)$ now gives the displayed formula for $\|u\|_Q^2$.

If $u=0$ in $L^2$, then step 2.2 says $\langle g_j,\varphi\rangle=0$ for every $\varphi\in D_0$; this pairing is continuous by [F3] and $D_0$ is dense by [F4], so it vanishes on all of $H_N$, and taking $\varphi=g_j$ gives $g_j=0$. Step 2.3 then gives $h=0$; the norm formula yields $\|[u_n]\|_Q=0$, so the embedding is injective. Finally its image contains $D_0$, which is dense in $H_N$ by [F4]; thus the continuous injection has dense image and all claims follow.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$.

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
Let $C$ be a cube of side $\delta>0$ and $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, with $u_C:=|C|^{-1}\int_Cu$. Expanding the square and using Fubini on the finite cube gives
$$\int_C|u-u_C|^2=\frac1{2|C|}\int_C\int_C|u(x)-u(y)|^2\,dx\,dy.$$
Telescope $u(x)-u(y)$ through the $N$ coordinate changes and use $|\sum_{j=1}^Nz_j|^2\le N\sum_j|z_j|^2$. For the $j$th change, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|D_j(x,y)|^2\le\delta\int_{\min(x_j,y_j)}^{\max(x_j,y_j)}|\partial_ju|^2$. For fixed values of the other coordinates and fixed $s\in[0,\delta]$, the measure of pairs $(x_j,y_j)$ whose segment contains $s$ is $2s(\delta-s)\le\delta^2/2$; integrating the displayed bound over the cube variables and dividing by $2|C|$ therefore yields the safe estimate
$$\|u-u_C\|_{L^2(C)}^2\le N\delta^2\sum_{j=1}^N\|\partial_j u\|_{L^2(C)}^2.$$
It applies to complex $u$ because the squared-modulus Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is used.

The estimate of step 1.1 passes to every $u\in Q$: approximate $u$ in the $Q$ norm by elements of $C_c^\infty$ (the defining completion), restrict to $C$, and use [F1] to pass the $L^2$ and derivative limits.

For $R>0$ and $u\in Q$, the coercive weight gives
$$\int_{|q|>R}|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\int_{|q|>R}c|q|^2|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\|u\|_Q^2.$$
Thus the $L^2$ tails of the $Q$ unit ball are uniformly small for large $R$.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $R$ so the squared tail in step 2.1 is below $\varepsilon^2/16$, and partition $[-R,R]^N$ into finitely many cubes of side $\delta$ so that the sum of the squared mean-approximation errors in step 1.2 is below $\varepsilon^2/16$. Replacing $u$ on each cube by its mean and setting it to zero outside the large cube then approximates every $u$ in the $Q$ unit ball to $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon/2$.

The resulting vectors of cube means lie in a bounded subset of a finite-dimensional complex coordinate space: $\|u\|_2\le\|u\|_Q\le1$ and each cube has fixed positive volume. Subdivide a bounded real-and-imaginary coordinate box into finitely many boxes of sufficiently small side length. The associated finitely many piecewise-constant functions approximate every vector of means to $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon/2$. Combining with step 2.2 gives a finite $\varepsilon$-net for the image of the $Q$ unit ball. Scaling shows that the image of every bounded $Q$ set is totally bounded.

Let $K$ be the $H_N$ closure of the image of the $Q$ unit ball. It is complete because it is closed in the complete space $H_N$, and it is totally bounded because a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net for the image is an $\varepsilon$-net for its closure. To prove compactness directly, suppose an open cover of $K$ has no finite subcover. At each $n\ge1$, take the explicit finite net from step 2.3 at radius $2^{-n-2}$; its closed balls of radius $2^{-n-1}$ cover $K$. Starting with $C_0=K$, choose the least ball index for which $C_n:=C_{n-1}\cap\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$ has no finite subcover. Such an index exists, since otherwise finitely many finite subcovers would cover $C_{n-1}$. Each $C_n$ is nonempty, closed, nested, and has diameter at most $2^{-n}$. For $m>n$, any point of nonempty $C_m$ lies in both selected balls, so $\|p_m-p_n\|_2\le2^{-m-1}+2^{-n-1}$; hence $(p_n)$ is Cauchy and converges to some $p\in H_N$. Since $C_n$ is nonempty and is contained in both $K$ and $\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$, the distance from $p_n$ to $K$ is at most $2^{-n-1}$. Therefore $\operatorname{dist}(p,K)\le\|p-p_n\|_2+2^{-n-1}\to0$; closedness of $K$ gives $p\in K$. For fixed $n$ and each $m>n$, $C_m\subseteq C_n$ and $C_m\subseteq\overline B(p_m,2^{-m-1})$, so $\inf_{y\in C_n}\|p_m-y\|_2\le2^{-m-1}$. The triangle inequality gives $\inf_{y\in C_n}\|p-y\|_2\le\|p-p_m\|_2+2^{-m-1}\to0$; since $C_n$ is closed, $p\in C_n$. An open set of the cover containing $p$ contains $K\cap B(p,r)$ for some $r>0$; for large $n$, $\operatorname{diam}(C_n)<r$, so that one open set covers $C_n$, a contradiction. Thus $K$ is compact. The net grids are explicitly indexed by finite integer boxes, and each recursive ball choice is the least admissible index; no choice beyond the inherited countable foundation is used.
Step 3.1 proves that the closed-unit-ball image under $J$ has compact closure; applying the equivalent criterion in [F2] to the linear inclusion proves that $J:Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ is compact.

and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $d\ge1$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ put $K_j^y:=L^2(\mathbb R,dy_j)$ and take a copy $(g^{(j)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of the Hermite family of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $K_j^y$. Define the left-associated completed tensor products by $\mathcal K_1^y:=K_1^y$ and $\mathcal K_r^y:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^y\widehat\otimes K_r^y$ for $2\le r\le d$. Let $\Theta_y^{(1)}:K_1^y\to L^2(\mathbb R,dy_1)$ be the identity; recursively, for $2\le r\le d$, let

$$\Theta_y^{(r)}:=\Theta_{r-1,1}^y\circ\bigl(\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}\bigr):\mathcal K_r^y\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy),$$

where $\Theta_{r-1,1}^y:L^2(\mathbb R^{r-1},dy)\widehat\otimes K_r^y\to L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy)$ is the two-factor Euclidean product unitary of [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]], and $\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}$ is the bounded tensor map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Thus $\Theta_y^{(r)}$ is a specified unitary, with $\Theta_y^{(r)}(u\otimes v)(y',y_r)=\Theta_y^{(r-1)}u(y')v(y_r)$ almost everywhere. For $N=(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d$, set $G_N^{y,1}:=g^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{y,r}:=G_N^{y,r-1}\otimes g^{(r)}_{n_r}$; define $g_N:=\Theta_y^{(d)}G_N^{y,d}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$.

Let $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^d$ list the multi-indices by increasing total degree $M=\sum_jn_j$ and, within each finite level, in lexicographic order. By [[thm-stars-and-bars]] each level is finite and the levels exhaust $\mathbb N^d$, so this specifies a bijection. All sums indexed by $\mathbb N^d$ below are taken in this order; nonnegative sums equivalently mean the supremum of finite subsums.

The functions $g_N$ have smooth product representatives from the recursive construction. These representatives are unique: a continuous difference that is nonzero at a point remains nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. The coordinate derivatives in (b) and (c) are taken on these representatives and their scaled products.

Then:

(a) $(g_N)_{N\in\mathbb N^d}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$: $\langle g_N,g_M\rangle=\delta_{NM}$ and every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$ has $f=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\langle f,g_N\rangle g_N$ with $\|f\|^2=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2$, the sum being the supremum over finite subfamilies ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]);

(b) with the eigenvalues $\lambda_N:=\sum_{j=1}^d(2n_j+1)=2M+d$, $M:=\sum_jn_j$, let $A_d$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $e_m:=g_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $\lambda_{\varphi(m)}$. Then $A_d$ is self-adjoint with

$$A_dg_N=\lambda_Ng_N,\qquad D(A_d)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\lambda_N^2|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(A_d)=\{2M+d:M\in\mathbb N\}$$

(the spectrum by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]); the algebraic span of the $g_N$ is a core, and on that span

$$A_d=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(-\partial_{y_j}^2+y_j^2\bigr)$$

as operators, the $j$-th summand acting in the $j$-th coordinate;

(c) for real $m_j,\omega_j,\hbar>0$ put $\ell_j:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_j\omega_j)}$ and let $D_j:K_j^y\to K_j^x:=L^2(\mathbb R,dx_j)$ be the one-dimensional unitary of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]. Define $\mathcal K_1^x:=K_1^x$ and $\mathcal K_r^x:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^x\widehat\otimes K_r^x$ for $2\le r\le d$, and define $\Theta_x^{(1)}$ and $\Theta_x^{(r)}$ by the same recursion as $\Theta_y^{(r)}$, using the two-factor Euclidean product unitaries on the $x$-coordinate spaces. Let $\mathcal D_1:=D_1$ and recursively $\mathcal D_r:=\mathcal D_{r-1}\otimes D_r:\mathcal K_r^y\to\mathcal K_r^x$; each $\mathcal D_r$ is unitary by [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Put $D_d:=\Theta_x^{(d)}\mathcal D_d(\Theta_y^{(d)})^{-1}:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)$. For $N\in\mathbb N^d$, define $G_N^{x,1}:=D_1g^{(1)}_{n_1}=:\psi^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{x,r}:=G_N^{x,r-1}\otimes\psi^{(r)}_{n_r}$; then $\psi_N:=D_dg_N=\Theta_x^{(d)}G_N^{x,d}$. Let $H$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $\psi_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $E_{\varphi(m)}$, where $E_N:=\hbar\sum_{j=1}^d\omega_j(n_j+\frac12)$. Then $H$ is self-adjoint with

$$H\psi_N=E_N\psi_N,\qquad D(H)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_N E_N^2|\langle f,\psi_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(H)=\overline{\{E_N:N\in\mathbb N^d\}},$$

the span of the $\psi_N$ is a core, and on that core

$$H=\sum_{j=1}^d\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_j}\partial_{x_j}^2+\frac{m_j\omega_j^2}{2}x_j^2\Bigr);$$

(d) if $\omega_1=\cdots=\omega_d=\omega$, then $\sigma(H)=\{\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2):M\in\mathbb N\}$, and the eigenvalue $\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2)$ has multiplicity

$$\bigl|\{(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d:n_1+\cdots+n_d=M\}\bigr|=\binom{M+d-1}{d-1};$$

in particular for $d=3$ the multiplicity is $(M+1)(M+2)/2$ ([[thm-stars-and-bars]]). All parameters are positive real numbers; no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

derivations.claim: In [F2] choose $\hbar=1$, $m_j=(2a_j)^{-1}$ and $\omega_j=2\sqrt{a_jc}$. Then $\hbar^2/(2m_j)=a_j$ and $m_j\omega_j^2/2=c$. The eigenvalue from [F2] in coordinate $j$ is $\omega_j(n_j+1/2)=(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}$. Summing over the $N$ coordinates gives the displayed differential eigenvalue $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}$. In the same scaling, $b_j=m_j\omega_j=\sqrt{c/a_j}$ and the normalized $n_j=0$ Gaussian becomes $(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}$; taking the product gives the stated ground representative.

Each product Hermite function is a polynomial times a Gaussian, so it and all first derivatives have finite squared integrals after multiplication by any fixed polynomial. Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\chi_R(q)=\chi(q/R)$ with $\chi=1$ on $|q|\le1$, $\chi=0$ on $|q|\ge2$, and $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. Such a $\chi$ can be formed from $\eta(s)=e^{-1/s}$ for $s>0$ and $\eta(s)=0$ for $s\le0$, by taking $\chi(q)=\eta(4-|q|^2)/(\eta(4-|q|^2)+\eta(|q|^2-1))$. Then $0\le\chi_R\le1$ and $\chi_R\psi_{\mathbf n}\in C_c^\infty$. The weighted-function error is supported on $|q|>R$ and bounded in squared integral by the integrable tail $(c|q|^2+2)|\psi_{\mathbf n}|^2$, so its $L^2$ norm tends to zero. For each derivative,
$$\partial_j((1-\chi_R)\psi_{\mathbf n})=(1-\chi_R)\partial_j\psi_{\mathbf n}-(\partial_j\chi_R)\psi_{\mathbf n};$$
the first term tends to zero by its Gaussian tail and the second has norm at most $C\|\psi_{\mathbf n}\|_2/R$. Thus $\chi_R\psi_{\mathbf n}$ converges in the form norm, proving $\psi_{\mathbf n}\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$.

For $v\in C_c^\infty$, integration by parts and the eigenvalue identity in step 1.1 give
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(\psi_{\mathbf n},v)=(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2)
\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},v\rangle.$$
The left side is continuous in the form norm of $v$ by Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and the right side is continuous since $\|v\|_2\le\|v\|_{Q_{\mathrm{osc}}}$. Density of $C_c^\infty$ in its defining completion extends the identity to every $v\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. Taking $v=\psi_{\mathbf m}$ proves that $\xi_{\mathbf n}:=(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2)^{-1/2}\psi_{\mathbf n}$ is orthonormal in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. If $u\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is orthogonal in this form inner product to every $\xi_{\mathbf n}$, conjugating the displayed identity gives $\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle=0$ for every $\mathbf n$. Completeness in $L^2$ from [F2] makes the image of $u$ zero, and the injective inclusion in [F1] makes $u=0$ in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. Thus $(\xi_{\mathbf n})$ is complete there.

Parseval in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ with the complete orthonormal family $(\xi_{\mathbf n})$ gives
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,u)=\sum_{\mathbf n}(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2)
|\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
Parseval in $L^2$ gives $\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{\mathbf n}|\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2$. Subtracting $2\|u\|_2^2$ from the first identity yields the asserted expansion of the unshifted oscillator form.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Assume the finite-dimensional coercive form data and Hilbert space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]. The inclusion
$J:Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ is compact: the closure in $H_N$ of the image of
every bounded subset of $Q$ is compact in the metric topology. The proof below
uses an explicit cube-mean approximation for each finite $N$ and does not
assume a general Rellich theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$.

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then

$$M^{\perp\perp}=\overline{M},$$

where $\overline M$ is the norm closure of $M$ and $M^{\perp\perp}=(M^\perp)^\perp$.

derivations.claim: For fixed $f\in H_N$, the functional $v\mapsto\langle v,f\rangle_{H_N}$ is linear and satisfies $|\langle v,f\rangle|\le\|v\|_2\|f\|_2\le\|v\|_Q\|f\|_2$ by [F1] and Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus [F3] applied to the Hilbert space $(Q,a)$ gives a unique $Rf\in Q$ with the stated variational identity. For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$, conjugate-linearity in the second argument gives $a(v,\alpha Rf+\beta Rg)=\langle v,\alpha f+\beta g\rangle$, so uniqueness makes $R$ linear.

Taking $v=Rf$ in the identity gives $\|Rf\|_Q^2=a(Rf,Rf)=\langle Rf,f\rangle$. Hence $\|Rf\|_Q^2\le\|Rf\|_2\|f\|_2\le\|Rf\|_Q\|f\|_2$, so $\|Rf\|_Q\le\|f\|_2$ (with the zero case immediate). Consequently $R:H_N\to H_N$ is bounded by [F5].

The same identity and $a(Rf,Rf)\ge2\|Rf\|_2^2$ give $2\|Rf\|_2^2\le\|Rf\|_2\|f\|_2$; division when $Rf\ne0$ yields $\|R\|\le\tfrac12$. If $Rf=0$, the variational identity says $\langle v,f\rangle=0$ for every $v\in Q$; since $Q$ is dense in $H_N$ by [F1], continuity of the inner product gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$. Thus $R$ is injective.

For $f,g\in H_N$, the variational identity and conjugate symmetry of $a$ yield $\langle Rf,g\rangle=a(Rf,Rg)=\langle f,Rg\rangle$, so $R$ is self-adjoint by [F7]. Also $\langle Rf,f\rangle=a(Rf,Rf)\ge0$, so it is positive.

The map $f\mapsto Rf$ is bounded from $H_N$ into $Q$ by step 1.2, and the inclusion $J:Q\to H_N$ is compact by [F2]. Therefore for every bounded $B\subseteq H_N$, $R(B)=J(R(B))$ has compact closure, which is exactly compactness by [F6].

If $z\perp\operatorname{ran}R$, then $\langle Rf,z\rangle=0$ for every $f\in H_N$. Self-adjointness from step 2.2 gives $\langle f,Rz\rangle=0$ for every $f$, so $Rz=0$ and step 2.1 gives $z=0$. Thus $(\operatorname{ran}R)^\perp=\{0\}$, and [F8] gives $\overline{\operatorname{ran}R}=(\operatorname{ran}R)^{\perp\perp}=\{0\}^\perp=H_N$. Steps 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, 3.1, and 4.1 establish every stated property of $R$.

real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$

3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$

   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$

   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

Throughout this page $H$ is a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with
inner product linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

A **(possibly unbounded) linear operator on $H$** is a linear map
$T:D(T)\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]) whose **domain** $D(T)\subseteq H$ is a linear
subspace ([[def-linear-subspace]]). The domain is part of the data: $T=S$ means
$D(T)=D(S)$ and $Tx=Sx$ for all $x\in D(T)$. One writes $T\subseteq S$, and
calls $S$ an **extension** of $T$, when $D(T)\subseteq D(S)$ and $Sx=Tx$ for
every $x\in D(T)$.

The **graph** of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T):=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}\subseteq H\oplus H .$$
The direct sum $H\oplus H$ is read as the complex vector space of pairs with
coordinatewise operations and the inner product
$\langle (x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle$, whose induced
norm is
$$\|(x,y)\|=(\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2)^{1/2};$$
it is complete because $H$ is ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). The **graph norm**
on $D(T)$ is
$$\|x\|_T:=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2},$$
so that $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$
onto $\Gamma(T)$ with the norm restricted from $H\oplus H$.

$T$ is **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of $H\oplus H$. A linear
operator is determined by its graph, and the following elementary translations
are used silently below: $\Gamma(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H\oplus H$;
$\Gamma(T)\cap(\{0\}\oplus H)=\{(0,0)\}$; the image of $\Gamma(T)$ under the
first coordinate projection is $D(T)$; and $T\subseteq S$ if and only if
$\Gamma(T)\subseteq\Gamma(S)$. In particular a closed operator is exactly one
whose graph is a closed subspace of $H\oplus H$.

**Notation.** No boundedness of $T$ is assumed, and $T$ is frequently called
*unbounded* to stress this; a bounded everywhere defined operator on $H$ is the
special case $D(T)=H$ in which $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subspace by continuity.
The letter $I$ denotes the identity operator on $H$ with domain $H$.

**Completeness of $H\oplus H$.** If $(x_n,y_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in
$H\oplus H$, then $\|x_n-x_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ and
$\|y_n-y_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ show that $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are Cauchy
in $H$; let $x,y$ be their limits. Then
$\|(x_n,y_n)-(x,y)\|^2=\|x_n-x\|^2+\|y_n-y\|^2\to0$, so $H\oplus H$ is
complete. Consequently a sequence in $H\oplus H$ converges exactly when its two
coordinate sequences converge in $H$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $R$ is compact and self-adjoint. Applying [F2] and using $\ker R=\{0\}$ shows that the closed span of its nonzero eigenspaces is all of $H_N$. If $R\psi=\mu\psi$ with $\psi\ne0$, then $\mu\|\psi\|^2=\langle R\psi,\psi\rangle\ge0$ by positivity, while injectivity rules out $\mu=0$; hence every nonzero eigenvalue is positive.

Each eigenspace is finite-dimensional by [F2], and so has an orthonormal basis by [F3]. The set of nonzero eigenvalues is at most countable, and [A1] selects these finite bases; their union is an orthonormal family whose closed span is $H_N$ by step 1.1. The space is infinite-dimensional: the indicators of the pairwise disjoint unit cubes $[r,r+1)\times[0,1)^{N-1}$, $r\in\mathbb N$, are nonzero mutually orthogonal $L^2$ vectors. Thus the family can be indexed by $n\ge1$. The bound $\|R\|\le\tfrac12$ gives $0<\mu_n\le\tfrac12$ and $E_n\ge1$. The compact spectral theorem says only finitely many eigenvalues satisfy $\mu\ge\varepsilon$ for each $\varepsilon>0$; recursively taking a largest remaining eigenvalue (which exists because above half its positive supremum there are only finitely many) orders them nonincreasingly with multiplicity and gives $\mu_n\to0$, hence $E_n\to\infty$.

The family $(\psi_n)$ is complete by step 1.1, so [F4] gives $u=\sum_n\langle u,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n$ in norm for every $u\in H_N$ and Parseval. In particular $D(S)$ is dense because it contains all finite linear combinations of the $\psi_n$. Since each $E_n$ is real, the diagonal formula for $S$ gives $\langle Su,v\rangle=\langle u,Sv\rangle$ for finite sums, and then for all $u,v\in D(S)$ by [F7] and convergence of the coefficient series; thus $S$ is symmetric. For $u\in D(S)$ with coefficients $c_n$, Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] makes $\sum_nE_n|c_n|^2$ absolutely convergent, and step 1.2 gives $E_n\ge1$, so $\langle Su,u\rangle=\sum_nE_n|c_n|^2\ge\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|u\|_2^2$.

To compute the adjoint domain, let $v=\sum_nd_n\psi_n\in D(S^*)$ and write $S^*v=z=\sum_nz_n\psi_n$. Testing the adjoint identity on each $\psi_n$ gives $z_n=E_nd_n$. Because $z\in H_N$, Parseval gives $\sum_nE_n^2|d_n|^2<\infty$, so $v\in D(S)$. Conversely, if this sum is finite, then $z:=\sum_nE_nd_n\psi_n\in H_N$ and the coefficient identity $\langle Su,v\rangle=\langle u,z\rangle$ holds first for finite sums and then for every $u\in D(S)$ by [F7]; hence $v\in D(S^*)$ and $S^*v=Sv$. Therefore $D(S^*)=D(S)$ and $S^*=S$ as operators; by the unbounded self-adjointness definition in [F5], $S$ is self-adjoint.

On each $\psi_n$, $(S+I)^{-1}\psi_n=(E_n+1)^{-1}\psi_n=\mu_n\psi_n=R\psi_n$. Both sides are bounded operators on $H_N$ and agree on the span of the complete family, so they agree on all of $H_N$. Thus $(S+I)^{-1}=R$, which is compact by [F1].

The variational identity for $R$, applied to $f=\psi_n$, gives $a(v,R\psi_n)=\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ for every $v\in Q$. Since $R\psi_n=\mu_n\psi_n$ and $\mu_n>0$, each $\psi_n$ lies in $Q$ and
$$a(v,\psi_n)=\mu_n^{-1}\langle v,\psi_n\rangle.$$
Thus $\xi_n:=\sqrt{\mu_n}\,\psi_n$ is an orthonormal family in $Q$. If $v\in Q$ is orthogonal in $a$ to every $\xi_n$, the displayed identity makes all $H_N$ coefficients $\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ zero. The $H_N$ completeness of $(\psi_n)$ and injectivity of $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ force $v=0$ in $Q$. Hence $(\xi_n)$ is complete in $Q$, and Parseval in $(Q,a)$ gives
$$a(v,v)=\sum_n\mu_n^{-1}|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2=\sum_n(E_n+1)|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$

Parseval in $H_N$ gives $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_n|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2$. Subtracting $(C_0+2)$ times this identity from step 2.3 yields the claimed formula for $q_h(v)$, because $E_n+1-(C_0+2)=E_n-C_0-1=\lambda_n$.

If $u\in D(h)=D(S)$ and $c_n=\langle u,\psi_n\rangle$, then $\sum_nE_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$ by the definition of $D(S)$. Since $E_n\ge1$, $E_n+1\le2E_n^2$, so $\sum_n(E_n+1)|c_n|^2<\infty$. Step 2.3 therefore gives $u\in Q$. Thus every eigenvector, and indeed every operator-domain vector, belongs to the form domain.

The domains defined by the squared coefficient sums for $E_n$ and $\lambda_n=E_n-(C_0+1)$ coincide. Indeed
$$\lambda_n^2\le2E_n^2+2(C_0+1)^2,\qquad E_n^2\le2\lambda_n^2+2(C_0+1)^2.$$
Multiplying by $|c_n|^2$ and summing preserves finiteness in both directions because $\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|u\|_2^2<\infty$ by [F4]. This proves the displayed coefficient-domain description of $D(h)$.

Let $u\in C_c^\infty$ and set $f:=(-\sum_ja_j\partial_j^2+W+1)u\in H_N$. Integration by parts gives $a(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for $v\in C_c^\infty$; both sides are continuous in $v$ for the $Q$ norm by [F7], and $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $Q$, so the identity holds for all $v\in Q$. It is the defining variational identity for $Rf$, and uniqueness in [F1] gives $Rf=u$. Hence $u\in\operatorname{ran}R=D(S)$ and $(S+I)u=f$, so $Su=-\sum_ja_j\partial_j^2u+Wu$.

Subtracting the real scalar $(C_0+1)I$ preserves self-adjointness on the same domain, and $E_n\ge1$ gives eigenvalues $\lambda_n=E_n-C_0-1\ge-C_0$. For $u\in D(h)$, the diagonal expansion and Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] make $\langle hu,u\rangle=\sum_n\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2$ absolutely convergent; Parseval then gives $\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$. The lowest eigenvalue corresponds to the largest eigenvalue $\mu_1$ of $R$; its eigenspace is nonzero and finite-dimensional by [F2]. Since $W=V+C_0+1$, step 3.1 shows that $h=S-(C_0+1)I$ extends the specified polynomial differential expression. Finally $h+(C_0+2)I=S+I$, whose inverse is the compact operator $R$ by step 2.2. These statements establish the declared realization and all listed scope limits.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of
[[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]. Its variational operator $R$
is compact, self-adjoint, positive, and injective on the infinite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space $H_N$. Let $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ be its positive eigenvalues
in nonincreasing order, with multiplicity, and choose corresponding
orthonormal eigenvectors $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$. Put
$E_n:=\mu_n^{-1}-1$ and define
$$D(S):=\left\{u=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\psi_n\in H_N:\sum_{n\ge1}E_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad Su:=\sum_{n\ge1}E_nc_n\psi_n.$$
The series for $u$ converges in $H_N$ by the Hilbert-space expansion theorem.
Then $S$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\langle Su,u\rangle\ge\|u\|_2^2$
for every $u\in D(S)$; also $(S+I)^{-1}=R$ is compact. For every
$u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
$$Su=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Wu.$$
Consequently $h:=S-(C_0+1)I$, on the same domain, is a self-adjoint realization
of the differential expression in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]] and satisfies
$\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$ for every $u\in D(h)$.
It has compact resolvent, meaning that for some $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
$h-zI:D(h)\to H_N$ is bijective with bounded inverse on $H_N$, and that
inverse is compact; here $z=-(C_0+2)$ and $(h+(C_0+2)I)^{-1}=R$. Put
$\lambda_n:=E_n-C_0-1$, the eigenvalues of $h$; equivalently,
$$D(h)=\left\{u=\sum_nc_n\psi_n:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $u\in Q$,
$$a(u,u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(E_n+1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2,\qquad
q_h(u):=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2
=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The lowest eigenvalue is attained and has finite multiplicity. This selects a
form realization; it does not assert that the differential expression on
$C_c^\infty$ is essentially self-adjoint or that it has no other self-adjoint
extensions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Parseval gives $\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|f\|^2$. Since $|e^{-it\lambda_n}|=1$, the finite partial sums defining $U(t)f$ are Cauchy in $H_N$, so converge; Parseval gives $\|U(t)f\|^2=\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|f\|^2$. The coefficient formula shows $U(-t)U(t)f=f=U(t)U(-t)f$ and $U(s)U(t)f=U(s+t)f$, first on finite sums and then on all of $H_N$ by norm convergence and the norm bound. Thus $U(t)$ is a surjective isometry, hence unitary, and $U(0)=I$.

Fix $s\in\mathbb R$ and $f\in H_N$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite set $F\subset\mathbb N$ with $\sum_{n\notin F}|c_n|^2<\varepsilon^2/64$, possible by convergence of the nonnegative series in [F2]. The norm of the difference on the complement is at most $2(\sum_{n\notin F}|c_n|^2)^{1/2}<\varepsilon/4$. On the finite set $F$, each scalar $e^{-it\lambda_n}$ is continuous in $t$, so the finite partial difference has norm below $3\varepsilon/4$ for $t$ sufficiently close to $s$. The triangle inequality proves $\|U(t)f-U(s)f\|<\varepsilon$, establishing strong continuity.

Let $f\in D(h)$, so $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$. Since $|e^{-it\lambda_n}|=1$, $U(t)f$ has the same finite weighted coefficient sum and belongs to $D(h)$. For $r\ne0$,
$$\frac{U(t+r)f-U(t)f}{r}
=\sum_ne^{-it\lambda_n}\frac{e^{-ir\lambda_n}-1}{r}c_n\psi_n.$$
The scalar integral identity $e^{-ir\lambda}-1=\int_0^r(-i\lambda)e^{-is\lambda}\,ds$ gives $|(e^{-ir\lambda}-1)/r|\le|\lambda|$. Thus the difference quotient coefficients are dominated in square sum by $\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2$. On each finite set they converge to $-i\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n$; choosing a finite set with small tail in that dominating series and then taking $r\to0$ proves convergence in $H_N$ to $-i\sum_n\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n\psi_n=-ihU(t)f$.

Conversely, suppose the norm derivative at $t=0$ exists and equals $g\in H_N$. Continuity of the coefficient functional $v\mapsto\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ from [F3] makes its value on the difference quotient converge to $-i\lambda_nc_n$. Hence $\langle g,\psi_n\rangle=-i\lambda_nc_n$ for every $n$. Parseval for $g$ implies $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2=\|g\|^2<\infty$, so $f\in D(h)$ by [F1]. If the derivative exists at any other $t$, the same coefficient argument multiplies each coefficient by a unit phase and yields the identical summability condition. Thus the differentiability domain is exactly $D(h)$ at every $t$.

be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
converges to $T$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-metric-convergence]]).  Here the displayed scalar series is, under the
library convention, the series of the sequence
$(\|u_{m+1}\|\,\|v_{m+1}\|)_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case
$$\|T\|_1=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|:\ R_m\to T\ \text{in operator norm}\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being over all such **nuclear representations** of $T$, with the
same zero-based shift understood in every displayed sum, and the
infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,
the singular-value series
$T=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ is a nuclear representation with
sum $\|T\|_1$.

([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$

equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$

   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$

3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);

   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,

real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

derivations.claim: Each $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}$ is finite, and only finitely many multi-indices have $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\le M$ for any real $M$: that inequality bounds every nonnegative integer $n_j$ by $M/(2\alpha_j)$. Hence their values can be listed in nondecreasing order with finite multiplicities; denote this list by $(\epsilon_k)_{k\ge0}$.

On $C_c^\infty$, the shifted interacting form has weight $V+C_0+2\ge c|q|^2+2$, so it dominates the shifted oscillator form from [F2]. Therefore a Cauchy sequence in $Q$ is Cauchy in the oscillator form norm; the identity map extends to a continuous map $Q\to Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, with the same $L^2$ representative because both completions inject into $H_N$ by [F3]. Subtracting the shifts in the two form norms gives
$$q_h(u)=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2\ge
q_{\mathrm{osc}}(u)-C_0\|u\|_2^2\qquad(u\in Q).$$

Fix $k\ge0$ and let $L_k=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_0,\ldots,\psi_k\}$. The linear map from $L_k$ to the span of the first $k$ oscillator eigenvectors, sending $u$ to its $k$ oscillator coefficients, has a nonzero kernel because $\dim L_k=k+1>k$. Choose $u\ne0$ in that kernel. Since $u$ lies in the span of the first $k+1$ interacting eigenvectors, [F1] gives $q_h(u)\le\lambda_k\|u\|_2^2$. Its oscillator coefficients at indices below $k$ vanish, so [F2] gives $q_{\mathrm{osc}}(u)\ge\epsilon_k\|u\|_2^2$. Step 1.2 now yields $\lambda_k\|u\|_2^2\ge q_h(u)\ge(\epsilon_k-C_0)\|u\|_2^2$, hence
$$\lambda_k\ge\epsilon_k-C_0.$$
This argument also covers $k=0$, when the span of zero oscillator vectors is $\{0\}$.

The diagonal coefficients $e^{-\beta\lambda_k}$ have finite sum by step 3.1. Thus the rank-one series for $\rho_\beta$ is trace class by [F4]; it is positive because
$$\langle\rho_\beta f,f\rangle
=\sum_ke^{-\beta\lambda_k}|\langle f,\psi_k\rangle|^2\ge0.$$
Applying [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta)=Z_\beta$. For bounded $B$, the functional $x\mapsto\langle Bx,\psi_k\rangle$ is linear and has norm at most $\|B\|$ by Cauchy--Schwarz and [F8]. By [F6] it is represented by a vector $w_k$ with $\|w_k\|\le\|B\|$ and $\langle Bx,\psi_k\rangle=\langle x,w_k\rangle$. Hence
$$\rho_\beta Bx=\sum_k\langle x,w_k\rangle e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\psi_k$$
is a nuclear representation with coefficient sum at most $\|B\|Z_\beta$. By [F4], $\rho_\beta B$ is trace class. Its basis trace in $(\psi_k)$ is absolutely convergent and equals the trace by [F7]. The $k$th diagonal entry is
$$\langle \rho_\beta B\psi_k,\psi_k\rangle
=e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle B\psi_k,\psi_k\rangle,$$
so this basis sum is the asserted numerator. Each term is bounded in modulus by $e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\|B\|$ by [F8] and $\|\psi_k\|=1$, giving the stated absolute bound. Division by $Z_\beta>0$ proves the expectation formula.

$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$

   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;

derivations.claim: Write $a_\lambda=q_\lambda+2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ for the shifted form inner product of the $\lambda$ completion. On $C_c^\infty$, $V_\lambda\ge V_0$ gives $a_\lambda(u,u)\ge a_0(u,u)$, so a $Q_\lambda$-Cauchy sequence is $Q_0$-Cauchy and the identity extends continuously to $Q_\lambda\to Q_0$ with the same $L^2$ representative. The unshifted forms $q_\lambda=a_\lambda-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ and $q_0=a_0-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ are continuous on their respective form spaces. For any $u\in Q_\lambda$, approximate it in $Q_\lambda$ by $u_r\in C_c^\infty$; then $q_\lambda(u_r)\ge q_0(u_r)$ for every $r$, and continuity of both forms gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)$ in the limit. For normalized $u\in Q_\lambda$, [F3] then gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)\ge E_g(0)$. Taking the infimum yields $E_g(\lambda)\ge E_g(0)$.

The Gaussian $\phi_b$ from [F2] and its derivative are polynomial times a Gaussian. For cutoffs $\chi_R$ as in the cutoff construction of
[[lem-qft-hermite-oscillator-research-supplier]], $\chi_R\phi_b\in C_c^\infty$
converges to $\phi_b$ in the $\lambda$ form norm: the derivative error is
$(1-\chi_R)\phi_b'-(\chi_R')\phi_b$, whose first term has vanishing Gaussian
tail and whose second has norm at most $C\|\phi_b\|_2/R$; the weighted error
has squared magnitude bounded by $(m^2q^2/2+\lambda q^4+2)|\phi_b|^2$, an
integrable polynomial-Gaussian tail. Thus $\phi_b\in Q_\lambda$.

Let $\mathbb E_b[g]:=\int g(q)\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2}\,dq$. The Hermite
ground function in [F2] is normalized, so $\mathbb E_b[1]=1$. On any compact
interval of positive $b$ values, the derivatives of the integrands through
order two are bounded by a constant times $(1+|q|^4)e^{-b_*q^2}$ for some
$b_*>0$, which is integrable; [F5] therefore permits differentiation under the
integral. Differentiating $\mathbb E_b[1]=1$ gives
$$0=\mathbb E_b\!\left[\frac1{2b}-q^2\right],\qquad
\mathbb E_b[q^2]=\frac1{2b}.$$
Differentiating the second identity and using
$\partial_b(\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2})=(\frac1{2b}-q^2)\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2}$ gives
$$-\frac1{2b^2}=\mathbb E_b\!\left[q^2\left(\frac1{2b}-q^2\right)\right]
=\frac1{4b^2}-\mathbb E_b[q^4],$$
so $\mathbb E_b[q^4]=3/(4b^2)$. Since $\phi_b'=-bq\phi_b$, this gives
$\|\phi_b'\|_2^2=b/2$. Hence
$$\|\phi_b\|_2^2=1,\quad \|\phi_b'\|_2^2=b/2,\quad
\int q^2|\phi_b|^2=1/(2b),\quad\int q^4|\phi_b|^2=3/(4b^2).$$
The unperturbed form value
is $ab/2+m^2/(4b)=m\sqrt{a/2}=E_g(0)$, using $b=m/\sqrt{2a}$, and the quartic
contribution is $3\lambda/(4b^2)=3a\lambda/(2m^2)$. The variational bound
[F3] applied to this normalized vector yields
$$E_g(\lambda)\le E_g(0)+\frac{3a\lambda}{2m^2}.$$
Combining with step 1.1 proves both inequalities, including $\lambda=0$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). A **finite-mode regulator** in this item is a fixed
finite nonempty label set $J$ with $N:=|J|\ge1$, a fixed enumeration of $J$ by
$\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and the real coordinate vector
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may name sites of a finite
lattice or finitely many modes; their geometry enters only through the chosen
polynomial below. No limit in $N$ is part of this definition.

Choose real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$, constants $c>0$ and $C_0\ge0$,
and a real polynomial $V\in\mathbb R[q_1,\ldots,q_N]$ such that
$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$
Let $H_N:=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with vectors identified up to almost
everywhere equality and inner product
$$\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}u(q)\overline{v(q)}\,dq,$$
linear in the first variable. Under Countable Choice this is a complex Hilbert
space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let
$D_0:=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, the smooth compactly supported
complex-valued functions. The associated **polynomial differential expression**
is the map
$$h_0:D_0\to H_N,\qquad h_0u:=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Vu.$$
It is well defined because each derivative of $u$ and the product $Vu$ are
smooth and compactly supported. Set $W:=V+C_0+1$, so
$W(q)\ge1+c|q|^2$. This definition specifies finite mathematical data and a
differential expression; it does not choose a self-adjoint operator domain or
assert a continuum or infinite-volume limit.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of
[[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]. Its variational operator $R$
is compact, self-adjoint, positive, and injective on the infinite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space $H_N$. Let $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ be its positive eigenvalues
in nonincreasing order, with multiplicity, and choose corresponding
orthonormal eigenvectors $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$. Put
$E_n:=\mu_n^{-1}-1$ and define
$$D(S):=\left\{u=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\psi_n\in H_N:\sum_{n\ge1}E_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad Su:=\sum_{n\ge1}E_nc_n\psi_n.$$
The series for $u$ converges in $H_N$ by the Hilbert-space expansion theorem.
Then $S$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\langle Su,u\rangle\ge\|u\|_2^2$
for every $u\in D(S)$; also $(S+I)^{-1}=R$ is compact. For every
$u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
$$Su=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Wu.$$
Consequently $h:=S-(C_0+1)I$, on the same domain, is a self-adjoint realization
of the differential expression in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]] and satisfies
$\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$ for every $u\in D(h)$.
It has compact resolvent, meaning that for some $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
$h-zI:D(h)\to H_N$ is bijective with bounded inverse on $H_N$, and that
inverse is compact; here $z=-(C_0+2)$ and $(h+(C_0+2)I)^{-1}=R$. Put
$\lambda_n:=E_n-C_0-1$, the eigenvalues of $h$; equivalently,
$$D(h)=\left\{u=\sum_nc_n\psi_n:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $u\in Q$,
$$a(u,u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(E_n+1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2,\qquad
q_h(u):=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2
=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The lowest eigenvalue is attained and has finite multiplicity. This selects a
form realization; it does not assert that the differential expression on
$C_c^\infty$ is essentially self-adjoint or that it has no other self-adjoint
extensions.

derivations.claim: The hypotheses in [F1] specify a single integer $N$, a single coordinate space $\mathbb R^N$, and a single potential $V$; they contain no indexed family with varying cutoff.

A convergence assertion for varying cutoffs requires at least a family of objects, a common comparison space or maps between the spaces, and a convergence relation. Neither those data nor a limiting object occur in [F1] or [F2]. Therefore the theorems establish only the stated fixed-$N$ operator properties. The absence of those hypotheses is not a proof of nonexistence of a limit in a separately specified model.
